subject: Immunology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with longstanding Sjogren syndrome presents with new painless swelling of both parotid glands. Biopsy of a parotid mass shows a monoclonal proliferation of small lymphocytes with plasmacytoid features, and serum protein electrophoresis reveals a single M spike. Flow cytometry of the infiltrate is performed.
question: Which cell surface marker profile best characterizes the malignant cells in this patient?

options.text: Surface immunoglobulin positive, CD19 positive, CD20 positive, cytoplasmic immunoglobulin negative
CD3 positive, CD4 positive, CD8 negative
CD138 positive, CD19 negative, CD20 negative, CD3 negative
CD56 positive, CD16 positive, CD3 negative
CD34 positive, TdT positive, cytoplasmic CD3 positive

explanation_correct: This patient has an extranodal marginal zone (MALT-type) B-cell lymphoma that has undergone plasmacytic differentiation, the classic complication of longstanding Sjogren syndrome in the parotid. Once a B cell terminally differentiates into a plasma cell, it loses the pan-B markers CD19 and CD20 and the surface B-cell receptor, and strongly expresses CD138 (syndecan-1). The clone's capacity to secrete immunoglobulin is what produces the serum M spike.

explanation_incorrect.A: This profile describes an intact naive or memory B cell that still bears surface immunoglobulin; plasma cells lose surface immunoglobulin, CD19, and CD20 as they commit to secretion.
explanation_incorrect.B: This pattern is a CD4+ helper T cell, which has nothing to do with a monoclonal B-cell proliferation derived from a parotid B-cell clone.
explanation_incorrect.D: CD56/CD16/CD3-negative describes an NK cell, which is a cytotoxic lymphocyte rather than an immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cell.
explanation_incorrect.E: CD34 and TdT mark hematopoietic stem cells or early lymphoblasts as seen in ALL, not mature CD138+ effector plasma cells.

educationalObjective: Plasma cells are CD138+ CD19- CD20- professional immunoglobulin secretors, and loss of CD20 explains why anti-CD20 therapy fails once B cells differentiate into plasma cells.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated because of recurrent pneumonia with encapsulated organisms. He has normal B-cell numbers and normal immunoglobulin G levels, but cannot mount any antibody response to protein or polysaccharide vaccines over many years. Workup shows he lacks only CD4+ helper T cells and normal B-cell signaling.
question: Which B-cell process is directly dependent on CD4+ T follicular helper cells and therefore impaired in this patient?

options.text: Production of B-cell receptor through V(D)J recombination
Class switching from IgM to IgG and production of high-affinity antibody
Expression of CD19 on the B-cell surface
Elimination of autoreactive B cells by negative selection in the bone marrow
Formation of the B-cell repertoire through allelic exclusion

explanation_correct: T-dependent antigens require cognate help from CD4+ T follicular helper cells delivering CD40L-CD40 and IL-4/IL-21 signals; this drives the germinal center reaction, class switching, somatic hypermutation, and affinity maturation. Without T-cell help the B cell can still produce low-affinity IgM but switches poorly, so this boy fails to make specific IgG. This is the immune defect underlying profound T-cell deficiency states such as DiGeorge syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: V(D)J recombination of heavy and light chains is intrinsic to developing B cells in the bone marrow and is independent of T cells.
explanation_incorrect.C: CD19 is a pan-B marker expressed during B-cell development and does not require CD4+ help.
explanation_incorrect.D: Central B-cell tolerance by negative selection occurs in the bone marrow and selects against autoreactivity, not a help-dependent process.
explanation_incorrect.E: Allelic exclusion produces a monoallelic B-cell receptor during development and is not dependent on T-cell help.

educationalObjective: CD4+ T follicular helper cells license B cells in germinal centers for class switching, somatic hypermutation, and affinity maturation, which is why T-cell defects cause poor antibody responses.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a flare and is started on belimumab, which neutralizes soluble BAFF. Over the next year her serum anti-double-stranded DNA titers fall and her total peripheral B-cell count drops, but she continues to have detectable antibody titers to tetanus and to previous Epstein-Barr virus infection.
question: Which antibody-producing cell population explains the persistence of her long-lived titers despite BAFF blockade?

options.text: Short-lived plasmablasts in the circulation that depend continuously on BAFF
Naive follicular B cells awaiting new antigen exposure
Tissue-resident memory T cells in the bone marrow
Long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow that do not require BAFF for survival
Transitional B cells completing negative selection in the spleen

explanation_correct: BAFF (BLyS) supports survival and maturation of transitional and naive B cells, which is why belimumab therapy lowers peripheral B-cell counts and new autoantibody production. However, long-lived plasma cells that have migrated to bone marrow niches depend on stromal IL-6 and APRIL rather than BAFF, so preexisting protective titers persist. This distinction explains why antibody-depleting strategies often trim new autoimmunity without wiping out vaccine immunity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Plasmablasts are short-lived and highly BAFF-dependent, so they cannot account for stable titers persisting months to years after the drug starts.
explanation_incorrect.B: Naive follicular B cells do not secrete antibody at all; they are the precursors that must first be activated by antigen.
explanation_incorrect.C: Memory T cells are lymphocytes of T lineage and do not produce protective antibody titers.
explanation_incorrect.E: Transitional B cells are immature B cells leaving the marrow; they do not carry the burden of long-lived antibody production.

educationalObjective: Long-lived plasma cells in bone marrow niches survive without BAFF/CD19 signaling, so established antibody titers persist even when B-cell depletion or BAFF blockade is used.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 63-year-old man has progressive fatigue, hypercalcemia, and lytic skull lesions. Bone marrow aspirate shows sheets of cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm, an eccentric nucleus, and a prominent perinuclear clearing. Serum immunoglobulin is high, but there is no peripheral lymphadenopathy and flow cytometry of peripheral blood is normal.
question: The cells in this marrow most likely arose from which lineage, and what explains their retained capacity in this lesion?

options.text: T lymphocyte, because of retained CD3 signaling
Myeloid precursor, because of retained primary granules
B cell that has undergone terminal differentiation into a plasma cell, because of retained immunoglobulin secretory machinery
Natural killer cell, because of retained perforin and granzyme
Dendritic cell, because of retained antigen presentation capacity

explanation_correct: The eosinophilic cytoplasm, eccentric nucleus, and perinuclear hof (Golgi) are the morphologic signatures of a plasma cell, and the sheet-like marrow replacement with lytic lesions is multiple myeloma. These neoplastic plasma cells derive from a post-germinal-center B-cell clone and retain a massively expanded rough endoplasmic reticulum dedicated to immunoglobulin secretion, which is why light chains appear in urine as Bence Jones protein.

explanation_incorrect.A: T-cell neoplasms such as T-ALL or lymphomas show lymph node and skin involvement and do not produce monoclonal immunoglobulin.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myeloid precursors have granules but no perinuclear hof and no M-protein; their equivalent disease is myeloid leukemia.
explanation_incorrect.D: NK cells are nonsecretory and mediate cytolysis; they do not produce an M spike or osteolytic lesions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dendritic cells are professional antigen-presenting cells that do not secrete large quantities of immunoglobulin.

educationalObjective: Multiple myeloma is a neoplasm of terminally differentiated plasma cells whose perinuclear Golgi and abundant rough ER reflect intense immunoglobulin synthesis.
